title: Detection Strategy for Downgrade System Image on Network Devices
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for Downgrade System Image on Network ...
summary: This detection strategy covers downgrading the system image on network devices, tracked as T1601.002, where an adversary replaces running firmware with an older version so that a known weakness in that version can be exploited, or so that security features introduced later are no longer present. It matters because a downgrade can silently undo years of hardening on routers, switches and firewalls that sit in front of everything else, and the change often survives routine reboots and configuration audits. The telemetry that makes detection possible includes authentication and configuration change audit records from the device, file transfer logs for image uploads over management protocols, checksum or version change records in the configuration management system, and syslog messages announcing a reboot or a version string change. In practice it fails because a routine firmware update and a downgrade look almost identical, and many organisations do not collect version history from network equipment at all.

beginner.definition: This rule looks for a network device that is moved back to an older software version. The software that runs a router or a firewall is called firmware or an image. The technique is a downgrade because the version number goes down instead of up.
beginner.whyItMatters: Older firmware usually has weaknesses that are already known to attackers. Returning a device to an old version puts those weaknesses back on your network edge. The change can look like ordinary maintenance, so it may sit unnoticed for months. Devices at the edge protect everything behind them, which makes the impact large.
howItWorks: The platform collects login and configuration change records from each network device.
It reads the reported firmware version from the device and stores the value over time.
A second feed shows image files transferred to the device over a management protocol.
The platform compares the new version with the version that was running before.
It flags a version that is older than the recorded one, or a checksum that no longer matches.
An alert fires when the change was not part of an approved maintenance window.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital that replaces a working fire alarm panel with an older model from the store room. The old panel still works, so nothing seems broken today. But it no longer meets the current safety code, and nobody notices until the day it matters. The downgrade itself was the warning.
takeaways: A version number that moves backwards is the key signal, so you must record versions over time.
Maintenance windows explain many changes, so compare every change with the approved plan.
Network devices need configuration logging, or this technique stays invisible.

objectives: Explain why an older firmware version is a security problem on a network device.
Describe how to keep a version history for network equipment.
Identify the log records that show an image was transferred to a device.
Separate an approved firmware update from an unauthorised downgrade.
State which device groups should be monitored first and why.
dataSources: Network device syslog messages announcing image change, image verification failure or reboot after upgrade
Authentication and command audit records from network devices showing privileged configuration sessions
Configuration management system records of the reported firmware version and image checksum per device over time
File transfer service logs for image uploads to network devices over management protocols
Simple Network Management Protocol polling records for the reported software version object identifier
logic: The pattern is a device reporting a software version that is lower than the last recorded version, arriving shortly after a privileged configuration session and an image transfer to that device. You must correlate the device identity, the previous version, the new version, the checksum, the acting account and the time of the change, because a scheduled upgrade performed by the network team in a change window is expected while a version decrease outside a window and from an unusual account is not. The malicious case is distinguished by direction and authorisation rather than by the transfer itself, since the mechanics of installing an image are the same in both cases.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Network Device Firmware Version Downgrade
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: syslog
# detection:
#   selection:
#     message|contains:
#       - 'image boot'
#       - 'software version'
#       - 'image install'
#   filter_window:
#     maintenance_window: 'approved'
#   condition: selection and not filter_window
# level: medium
falsePositives: An approved rollback after a new firmware release caused an outage or a performance problem
A device that boots a standby image after a failed upgrade and reports the older version temporarily
Replacement hardware provisioned with an older image from the vendor and updated during the next window
Lab or test devices that are deliberately moved between versions by the network team
tuningNotes: Build a version inventory first, with a nightly poll of the reported software version and image checksum for every managed device, and only then alert on a decrease, because without history the rule cannot tell direction. Add a filter for documented change windows and scope alerting to perimeter and internet-facing devices before extending it to the access layer. Narrowing to the perimeter keeps the alert volume low but leaves a downgraded access switch undetected until the next review, so retain a daily report on all version changes and inspect it as part of routine monitoring.
